title: The Homemade Pantry: 101 Foods You Can Stop Buying and Start Making: A Cookbook
description: Change the way you relate to food with 101 easy recipes for everyday basics that encourage you to ditch ultra-processed meals in favor of nourishing, homemade dishes, from the creator of the hit blog Eating From The Ground Up. “ The Homemade Pantry is the sort of book that makes you want to head straight for your kitchen.”—Heidi Swanson, author of Super Natural Every Day “This book is both practical and inspiring, authoritative and down to earth. Why not make my own hot sauce, mozzarella, or graham crackers? From now on, I know I will.”—Molly Wizenberg, author of A Homemade Life The Homemade Pantry was born of a tight budget, Alana Cernila’s love for sharing recipes with her farmers’ market customers, and a desire to enjoy a happy cooking and eating life with her young family. On a mission to kick their packaged-food habit, she learned that with a little determination, anything she could buy at the store could be made in her kitchen, and her homemade versions were more satisfying, easier to make than she expected, and much tastier. Here are her very approachable recipes for 101 everyday staples, organized by supermarket aisle—from crackers to cheese, pesto to sauerkraut, and mayonnaise to toaster pastries. Be inspired by warm mozzarella that is stretched, thick lasagna noodles rolled from flour and egg, and fresh tomato sauce that bubbles on the stove. Whether you’re trying a recipe for butter, potato chips, spice mixes, or ketchup, you’ll discover the magic and thrill that comes with the homemade pantry. With stories offering patient, humble advice, tips for storing homemade foods, and vibrant photography throughout, The Homemade Pantry is a celebration of food made from scratch and is sure to become your go-to source for making delicious staples in your home kitchen.

title: The Homemade Vegan Pantry: The Art of Making Your Own Staples [A Cookbook]
description: A guide to creating vegan versions of pantry staples--from dairy and meat substitutes such as vegan yogurt, mayo, bacon, and cheese, to dressings, sauces, cookies, and more. “ The Homemade Vegan Pantry makes world-class vegan dishes possible for everyone at every skill level.”—Isa Chandra Moskowitz, from the foreword Kitchen crafters know the pleasure of making their own staples and specialty foods, whether it's cultured sour cream or a stellar soup stock. It's a fresher, healthier, more natural approach to eating and living. Now vegans who are sick of buying over-processed, over-packaged products can finally join the homemade revolution. Studded with full-color photos, The Homemade Vegan Pantry celebrates beautiful, handcrafted foods that don't take a ton of time, from ice cream and pizza dough, to granola and breakfast sausage. Miyoko Schinner guides readers through the techniques for making French-style buttercreams, roasted tomatoes, and pasta without special equipment. Her easy methods make "slow food" fast, and full of flavor. title: The Homemade Pantry: Canning fruits and vegetables for a healthier, additive-free diet (Ho
description: Imagine opening your pantry to find jars of peaches at their peak, crisp-tasting vegetables ready for supper, and a little more of the harvest saved for the months ahead. The Homemade Pantry helps you make that vision part of everyday life, with a practical introduction to home canning that puts thoughtful planning and food safety first. Start by deciding what your household will actually use. Learn how season, ripeness, and produce quality can shape the results, how to estimate the jars and workspace a batch needs, and how to read a tested canning recipe before you begin. You’ll get familiar with the essential jars, lids, and tools, along with ways to keep your equipment and work area clean and organized. Then explore preserving fruits and vegetables, from preparing produce to understanding the role of sugar, syrup, and juice. Discover why most low-acid vegetables require pressure canning, why tomatoes call for careful attention to tested directions, and why changes to ingredients, jar size, or processing time can affect safety. The book also explains the difference between boiling-water and pressure canning, how altitude adjustments matter, and which tempting shortcuts to avoid. Your pantry’s usefulness doesn’t end when the jars cool. Learn how to check seals, label and store jars, keep a simple inventory, and use older jars first. You’ll also find guidance on recognizing signs of spoilage and responding safely—because questionable food should never be tasted to test it. With a little planning, home-canned fruit and vegetables can become convenient ingredients for everyday meals while helping you make better use of seasonal produce.
